questions: How do moral wronging, bad inference, inquiry methods, and changes in epistemic standards differ?

evidence.excerpt: This is how Descartes, for instance, is commonly understood to conceive of epistemic obligations (e.g., Plantinga 1993: 19–22), owing to his suggestive description of doxastic mistakes as a kind of “sin” (peccatum) we are “at fault” for (“Fourth Meditiation” of Meditations AT VII:58; CSM II:41).

Other defenders of epistemic deontologism do not maintain that the epistemic ought has any moral bearing (Feldman 1988; 2000), and they differ on whether deontologism requires voluntary control (Steup 2000 holds that it does; Feldman 2000 holds that it does not).

sources.annotation: Provides secondary accounts of doxastic wronging, responsibility, control, and contemporary practical reasons for belief.

evidence.excerpt: Gendler (2011) and Egan (2011) argue that implicit bias creates a conflict between our ethical and epistemic aims.

As Gendler puts it, if you live in a society structured by racial categories that you disavow, either you must pay the epistemic cost of failing to encode certain sorts of base-rate or background information about cultural categories, or you must expend epistemic energy regulating the inevitable associations to which that information—encoded in ways to guarantee availability—gives rise.
This “epistemic self-censorship on non-epistemic grounds” makes it putatively impossible for agents to be both rational and equitable (Gendler 2011: 55, 57).
The solution to the dilemma, then, is not ignorance, but the situation-specific regulation of stereotype accessibility.

sources.annotation: Surveys the contested ethical–epistemic dilemma concerning social knowledge, objections to its inevitability, and situation-specific accessibility; its moral-encroachment pointer is identified as a pointer.
